citations.excerpt: We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance. Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared to state-of-the-art detection systems, YOLO makes more localization errors but is less likely to predict false positives on background. Finally, YOLO learns very general representations of objects. It outperforms other detection methods, including DPM and R-CNN, when generalizing from natural images to other domains like artwork.

## Abstract

We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance.

Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared

### 4.1. Comparison to Other Real-Time Systems

Many research efforts in object detection focus on making standard detection pipelines fast. [5] [38] [31] [14] [17] [28] However, only Sadeghi et al. actually produce a detection system that runs in real-time (30 frames per second or better) [31]. We compare YOLO to their GPU implementation of DPM which runs either at 30Hz or 100Hz. While the other efforts don’t reach the real-time milestone we also compare their relative mAP and speed to examine the accuracy-performance tradeoffs available in object detection systems.

Fast YOLO is the fastest object detection method on PASCAL; as far as we know, it is the fastest extant object detector. With 52.7% mAP, it is more than twice as accurate as prior work on real-time detection. YOLO pushes mAP

## 6. Conclusion

We introduce YOLO, a unified model for object detection. Our model is simple to construct and can be trained directly on full images. Unlike classifier-based approaches, YOLO is trained on a loss function that directly corresponds to detection performance and the entire model is trained jointly.

Fast YOLO is the fastest general-purpose object detector in the literature and YOLO pushes the state-of-the-art in real-time object detection. YOLO also generalizes well to new domains making it ideal for applications that rely on fast, robust object detection.

The workspace contains two distinct works on real-time object detection: "You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection" (YOLO) and "DETRs Beat YOLOs on Real-time Object Detection" (RT-DETR). Below is a balanced comparison of their approaches, supported by evidence from the papers.

### **Similarities**

1. **End-to-End Learning Frameworks**  
   Both YOLO and RT-DETR frame object detection as a unified, end-to-end learning problem, eliminating the need for multi-stage pipelines.  
   - **YOLO**: "Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second... Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance."  
   - **RT-DETR**: "In this paper, we propose the Real-Time DEtection TRansformer (RT-DETR), the first real-time end-to-end object detector to our best knowledge that addresses the above dilemma."

2. **Focus on Real-Time Performance**  
   Both models are explicitly designed for real-time applications, emphasizing speed without sacrificing accuracy.  
   - **YOLO**: "Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors."  
   - **RT-DETR**: "RT-DETR-R50 / R101 achieves 53.1% / 54.3% AP on COCO and 108 / 74 FPS on T4 GPU, outperforming previously advanced YOLOs in both speed and accuracy."

---

### **Differences**

1. **Architectural Paradigm**  
   - **YOLO** uses a **CNN-based single-stage detector** that predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities in one evaluation. It divides the image into a grid and predicts objects per grid cell.  
     - Evidence: "We frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation."  
   - **RT-DETR** is a **Transformer-based end-to-end detector** that eliminates the need for Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) by using a set prediction approach.  
     - Evidence: "Recently, end-to-end Transformer-based detectors (DETRs) have provided an alternative to eliminating NMS. Nevertheless, the high computational cost limits their practicality... We propose RT-DETR to address this."

2. **Post-Processing and NMS Dependency**  
   - **YOLO** relies on **NMS** for filtering duplicate detections, which can introduce instability in speed and accuracy.  
     - Evidence: "However, we observe that the speed and accuracy of YOLOs are negatively affected by the NMS."  
   - **RT-DETR** is **NMS-free**, using a query-based decoding mechanism that directly outputs a set of predictions, improving inference stability.  
     - Evidence: "RT-DETR supports flexible speed tuning by adjusting the number of decoder layers to adapt to various scenarios without retraining... eliminating the inconvenience caused by two NMS thresholds."

3. **Error Profiles and Generalization**  
   - **YOLO** tends to make more **localization errors** but fewer false positives on background. It generalizes well to new domains like artwork.  
     - Evidence: "YOLO makes more localization errors but is less likely to predict false positives on background... It outperforms other detection methods when generalizing from natural images to other domains like artwork."  
   - **RT-DETR** improves accuracy through **uncertainty-minimal query selection**, enhancing initial query quality and reducing false negatives.  
     - Evidence: "We propose the uncertainty-minimal query selection to provide high-quality initial queries to the decoder, thereby improving accuracy."

4. **Speed-Accuracy Trade-off and Flexibility**  
   - **YOLO** offers speed through model variants (e.g., Fast YOLO), but accuracy is limited by grid-based prediction and NMS.  
   - **RT-DETR** allows **flexible speed tuning** without retraining by adjusting decoder layers, making it adaptable to different deployment scenarios.  
     - Evidence: "RT-DETR supports flexible speed tuning by adjusting the number of decoder layers to adapt to various scenarios without retraining."

---

### **Conclusion**

While both YOLO and RT-DETR aim to achieve real-time object detection with high accuracy, they differ fundamentally in architecture and post-processing. baseline.answer:
- The workspace contains only one paper: "You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection" (YOLO), which introduces a one-stage detector that processes images in a single network evaluation.
- One-stage detectors like YOLO are extremely fast, with the base model running at 45 FPS and a smaller version (Fast YOLO) achieving 155 FPS, making them suitable for real-time applications.
- YOLO frames object detection as a regression problem, directly predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities from full images, enabling end-to-end optimization.
- Compared to two-stage detectors such as R-CNN and DPM, YOLO is faster but tends to make more localization errors, though it is less likely to predict false positives on background.
- Two-stage detectors typically use a disjoint pipeline: first extracting features and then applying classifiers or localizers on sliding windows or region proposals, which makes them slower but often more accurate in localization.
- YOLO outperforms some two-stage systems like DPM and R-CNN when generalizing to non-natural image domains (e.g., artwork), suggesting stronger generalization due to its unified architecture.
- Fast YOLO achieves double the mAP of other real-time detectors at the time, highlighting the efficiency-accuracy trade-off favoring one-stage methods in speed-critical scenarios.

Uncertainties:
- The workspace lacks comparative studies or additional papers directly analyzing multiple one-stage and two-stage detectors, limiting broader conclusions.
- There is no information on more recent architectures (e.g., SSD, RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN) or modern performance benchmarks, so the current state of the one-stage vs two-stage debate beyond YOLO’s initial release is not represented.

## Abstract

We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance.

Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared

## 3. Comparison to Other Detection Systems

Object detection is a core problem in computer vision. Detection pipelines generally start by extracting a set of robust features from input images (Haar [25], SIFT [23], HOG [4], convolutional features [6]). Then, classifiers [36, 21, 13, 10] or localizers [1, 32] are used to identify objects in the feature space. These classifiers or localizers are run either in sliding window fashion over the whole image or on some subset of regions in the image [35, 15, 39]. We compare the YOLO detection system to several top detection frameworks, highlighting key similarities and differences.

baseline.answer:
In workspace `ws-pilot-od`, only one work is present: *You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection* (YOLO). However, to address the query on region proposal networks, a broader search identified two key works from the corpus: *Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks* and the closely related *Faster r-cnn: Towards real-time object detection with region proposal networks* (arXiv version). Below is a comparison of how each uses proposals, based on verifiable evidence.

- **Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks**  
  This work introduces a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares full-image convolutional features with the detection network, enabling nearly cost-free region proposals. The RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position, trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals. These proposals are then used by the Fast R-CNN detector for final object detection, forming a unified system where the RPN acts as an "attention" mechanism, telling the network where to look.  
  Source: *Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks*, Section 3.1.

- **You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection** (present in workspace)  
  In contrast, YOLO does not use region proposals at all. Instead, it frames object detection as a regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from the entire image in a single network evaluation. The system divides the image into an $S \times S$ grid, with each grid cell responsible for predicting $B$ bounding boxes and confidence scores. This unified design reasons globally about the image, avoiding the need for separate region proposal stages and enabling real-time speeds.  
  Source: *You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection*, Section 2. Unified Detection.

The two approaches represent fundamentally different paradigms: Faster R-CNN relies on a dedicated region proposal stage (RPN) to generate candidate regions, while YOLO eliminates proposals entirely, performing detection in one unified pass.

- **"You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection" (Redmon et al.)**  
  This work introduces YOLO, which **does not use region proposals**. Instead, it frames object detection as a single regression problem across the entire image, directly predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities in one network evaluation. The model divides the image into a grid and each grid cell predicts a fixed number of bounding boxes without relying on region proposals. This design allows YOLO to be extremely fast (45–155 fps) and to capture global context, reducing false positives on background.  
  > *“Unlike sliding window and region proposal-based techniques, YOLO sees the entire image during training and test time so it implicitly encodes contextual information about classes as well as their appearance.”*

- **Region Proposal-Based Methods (e.g., Fast R-CNN, R-CNN)**  
  While not directly present in the workspace, these are referenced as contrast. Traditional methods **rely heavily on region proposals**—using selective search or sliding windows to generate candidate regions, then classifying each region separately. This two-stage process is slower and may miss global context, leading to more background errors.  
  > *“Fast R-CNN, a top detection method [14], mistakes background patches in an image for objects because it can’t see the larger context.”*  
  > *“Current detection systems repurpose classifiers to perform detection... evaluate them at various locations and scales in a test image.”*

In summary, YOLO eliminates the need for explicit region proposals by using a unified, single-pass architecture, while traditional methods depend on region proposal networks to localize objects before classification.
